newsitem.title: USA: U.S. electricity debate to heat up this week.
newsitem.headline: U.S. electricity debate to heat up this week.

text.p: The first of several proposals to break up the last of the big U.S. regulated monopolies, electric utilities, is set to be released this week by Arkansas Democrat Sen. Dale Bumpers.
Although his will be the first bill this year seeking to overhaul the $200 billion market, the Senate side is unlikely to take up the legislation for several months.

Instead, the House is expected to set the pace, with Commerce Committee Chairman Thomas Bliley and energy panel chairman Dan Schaefer, both Republicans, pushing federal efforts to allow consumers to shop for power.

In contrast, Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee chairman Frank Murkowski of Alaska announced earlier this month that before tackling legislation he would hold a series of workshops starting in late February.

Rep. Schaefer of Colorado is preparing to reintroduce a sweeping electricity restructuring bill next week, and the Clinton administration is aiming to offer its own bill in time for House energy panel debates.
Schaefer plans to make few changes to a bill he offered last summer, which required all states to let consumers choose their own electricity suppliers by the end of 2000.
Meanwhile, he has been cultivating consumer support for his bill, touting the potential savings in electricity costs that could come with competition among power producers.

"We are ahead of where we wanted to be in building support," said Schaefer's spokeswoman Dana Perino, noting that groups such as school districts liked the idea of lowering their electricity costs, which run in the millions.
Schaefer and other advocates of consumer choice point to a Clemson University study which says the average household monthly electric bill could fall by 43 percent in the long run to less than $40.

Hailing a similar study by the conservative Heritage Foundation, House Commerce Committee Chairman Thomas Bliley said Monday that academics "seem to agree on the principle that competition in electric utility markets ... will lower prices, improve service, and enhance the reliability of America's electrical power supply."
Schaefer's staff said it was unclear how many hearings the panel would hold on legislation before voting on a bill, having held nine on the issue last year.
The House energy panel has a new senior Democrat, Rep. Ralph Hall of Texas, who has yet to fix his position.
"I'm willing to referee," said Hall. "I have friends on both sides."

"I don't have any definite feelings or intentions right now," he told Reuters, although he added that he was leaning against explicitly linking clean air laws and electricity deregulation, as his predecessor as ranking Democrat, Rep. Frank Pallone of New Jersey, had proposed.
Pallone plans to reintroduce his bill next month, an aide said.

While Republicans have pressed for more state control over a range of issues, Bliley and Schaefer are eager to push a federal law with a deadline for all states to meet, even with several states moving ahead to open the market to competition.
In an apparent reversal of roles, Energy Department officials have said they are leaning against mandating a specific deadline in the administration's legislation.
Hall said while he supported states' rights, "I realize there are some things you have to have federal oversight on."
